directions: Plant bare-root or container-grown rootstock liners in spring in well-drained soil in full sun, then bud a desired rose variety onto the young rootstock; Dr. Huey is grown as a vigorous budding understock, not typically for its own bloom. Bred in the early twentieth century and possessing dark crimson, once-blooming flowers of modest garden merit in its own right, this variety became, almost by accident, the overwhelming standard rootstock for commercially budded roses across the United States for most of the twentieth century, prized for vigorous, disease-tolerant root growth and ease of propagation from cuttings at commercial scale. Gardeners occasionally discover their grafted rose has reverted to blooming with Dr. Huey's own dark red, once-flowering blooms after the budded top has died back from cold, disease, or age, since the vigorous rootstock readily suckers and can eventually outcompete a weakened scion. Prune out any suckering canes bearing the distinctive once-blooming crimson flowers promptly to redirect the plant's energy back to the desired grafted rose variety, or budded named rose varieties directly onto young Dr. Huey rootstock for commercial-style propagation.
